question: What proportion of new fracture clinic referrals have a named consultant review documented within 24 hours of first presentation?
why: The 2026 BOASt moved the consultant review target to 24 hours. Corpus audits measured the old 72-hour target only ([1538] 6% → 100%, [1593] closed loop); none has measured 24 hours.

standard.source: BOASt Outpatient and on-call services for people with fractures or musculoskeletal injury (BOA, February 2026), standard 2
standard.wording: Patients must have their case reviewed by a named consultant within 24 hours of first presentation. This can be performed in person or virtually in a trauma meeting. The outcome of this review should be documented and a copy sent to the patient and GP.

pass: Documented review by a named consultant (in person, virtual fracture clinic or trauma meeting) with date and time no more than 24 hours after first presentation (ED or community arrival time).
population: Include: patients of any age referred from ED, MIU or GP to the fracture clinic or virtual fracture clinic (VFC). Exclude: patients admitted from ED.
sample: 40 consecutive referrals from the VFC or fracture clinic referral list over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: ED system (arrival time); VFC or trauma meeting list and EPR note (review time, consultant name).

template.note: Local study code only; keep the key separately
ED/MIU arrival or GP referral receipt

change: Add a mandatory 'reviewing consultant' and 'review time' field to the VFC outcome template, and add a weekend VFC or trauma-meeting review slot on the rota.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive referrals, same template.
close_loop: Present at the T&O governance meeting; if it works, make the VFC template fields mandatory trust-wide and report monthly to the trauma lead.
evidence: [1538] VFC introduction: 6% seen within 72 h → 100% (mean 1.3 days) (virtual fracture clinic)
[1593] consultant-level opinion before face-to-face: 96% → 99% (mandatory senior review rule)
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from ED system and EPR
area: Fracture clinic, outpatients, imaging, bone health and infection
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

The FLS reviews people who are recommended interventions to reduce risk of fracture 4-8 weeks after a treatment recommendation is made, and at 52 weeks to ensure that: lifestyle recommendations and treatment decisions are reassessed; where the decision has been taken to treat, it has been started and taken appropriately. referral to falls reduction programmes has been actioned if appropriate.

question: What proportion of radiology reports describing vertebral body height loss call it a 'vertebral fracture'?
why: National work shows low standard terminology and referral ([1583] 60.1% terminology, 2.6% onward referral; [1700]/[1701] improved after interventions). Local closed loops are rare.

standard.source: Royal Osteoporosis Society, Effective Secondary Prevention of Fragility Fractures: Clinical Standards for Fracture Liaison Services, version 3 (September 2025), Standard 1 (Identify), quoting ROS radiology reporting guidance
standard.wording: Guidance on identification and reporting of vertebral fractures is given by the ROS. This recommends that radiology: Review the spine in all images of the chest, abdomen and pelvis. Report vertebral fractures clearly using the term ‘vertebral fracture’. Recommend further assessment and management to reduce fracture risk.

pass: Report uses the words 'vertebral fracture' (not only 'wedge', 'collapse', 'height loss' or 'compression'). Whether it also recommends a bone health assessment is recorded as a secondary measure.
population: Include: CT or radiograph reports (chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine) in patients aged 50+ that mention wedge, compression, collapse, height loss or fracture of a vertebra. Exclude: acute high-energy trauma, known metastases.
sample: 40 consecutive matching reports from a RIS free-text search over the last 2 months.
data_source: RIS text search; report text; FLS database for referral.

change: Add a reporting macro in RIS ('Vertebral fracture at Tx. Recommend fracture risk assessment / FLS referral') and send an automatic copy to the FLS.

evidence: [1583] UK CT reports: recommended term 60.1%, onward referral 2.6%
[1701] moderate/severe VFF reported 26% → 32% (UK-wide interventions)

why: Sampling is poor ([1278] five samples 51.0%, separate instruments 9.8%, no re-audit). No closed loop in corpus.

standard.source: BOAST Fracture Related Infections (BOA, September 2019; still the current BOAST), 'Assessment of FRI' and 'Secondary fracture surgery'
standard.wording: When debridement is indicated 5 samples should be taken from around the fracture site for microbiological culture using separate sterile instruments and a no touch technique for each. In all chronic infections and when the diagnosis is in doubt in acute infections take 2 samples for histology.

pass: Five or more separate deep tissue samples received by microbiology from the operation, with separate instruments documented.

question: What proportion of non-septic patients with suspected acute prosthetic joint infection receive no antibiotics before deep tissue samples are taken?
why: Early blind antibiotics spoil cultures. The only corpus PJI audit [1301] was single-cycle and did not focus on this.

standard.source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (BOA, October 2023, updated April 2024), standard 4
standard.wording: A patient who is not septic should not be given antibiotics until appropriate deep tissue samples have been taken.

pass: First antibiotic dose time is after the time of joint aspiration or surgical deep sampling (or no antibiotics before sampling).
population: Include: adults presenting with suspected PJI of hip or knee replacement without sepsis. Exclude: patients meeting sepsis criteria on arrival.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 12 months, up to 40.
data_source: ED records; drug chart (antibiotic administration times); theatre or aspiration record; microbiology system.

question: What proportion of hip and knee replacement discharge summaries tell the patient who to contact if they suspect joint infection?
why: Late recognition of PJI delays care. No corpus audit checks infection contact advice in arthroplasty discharge documents.

standard.source: BOAST Acute Management of Peri-Prosthetic Joint Infection (BOA, October 2023, updated April 2024), standard 1
standard.wording: Guidance on who to contact and how to respond to a patient with suspected PJI should be readily available to Primary Care providers and Emergency department practitioners, and be included in discharge documentation.

pass: Discharge summary (or attached discharge leaflet, documented) names warning signs of infection and gives a specific contact (ward or arthroplasty phone number) plus the advice not to start antibiotics before orthopaedic review.

question: What proportion of limb operations under tourniquet have prophylactic antibiotic given before tourniquet inflation?
why: Tourniquet audits in corpus measured pressure and time ([1664], [1299]) and antibiotic audits measured choice and bundle ([1333]). None measured timing against inflation.

standard.source: NICE NG125 rec 1.2.15 (2008, NG125 published 2019, updated 2020)
standard.wording: Consider giving a single dose of antibiotic prophylaxis intravenously on starting anaesthesia. However, give prophylaxis earlier for operations in which a tourniquet is used.

pass: Antibiotic administration time is before the tourniquet inflation time (local policy may add a minimum gap, for example ≥5 minutes).
population: Include: trauma and elective limb operations with a tourniquet where prophylaxis is indicated. Exclude: cases with no prophylaxis indicated.
sample: 40 consecutive tourniquet cases over 2–3 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart (antibiotic time); theatre system or operation note (tourniquet inflation time).
